description_full: Rightmove plc, together with its subsidiaries, operates property portal in the United Kingdom and internationally. The company operates through Agency, New Homes, and Other segments. The Agency segment provides resale and lettings property advertising services, and rental operators advertising and rental services on its platforms. This segment also offers tenant referencing and rent guarantee insurance services to lettings agents and landlords. The New Homes segment provides property advertising services to new home developers and housing associations on its platforms. The Other segment offers commercial and overseas property advertising services; non-property advertising services that include third party advertising and data services; and mortgage services. The company serves property professionals, such as residential and commercial estate/letting agents, residential developers and operators, surveyors, lenders, mortgage lenders/brokers, home services providers, and other professionals. Rightmove plc was founded in 2000 and is based in Milton Keynes, the United Kingdom.

financial_summary: Rightmove Plc is a mid-cap communication services business with a $5.5B market cap on $562M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +11% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 508% against a 9% cost of capital — a 499-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $299M in free cash flow — roughly 53 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.09× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 5.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 3.3× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Operating margins softening -1.6pp YoY — early warning on the moat
Carries a 96% premium to sector median EV/EBITDA (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Advertising-cycle exposure and content/regulatory risk — a single platform policy shift or ad-spend contraction cascades through the P&L quickly.
Cord-cutting acceleration and audience fragmentation — legacy distribution bundles unravel faster than subscription revenue can replace them.
AI-generated content commoditisation — as creation costs collapse toward zero, content libraries lose pricing power and differentiation narrows.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 59% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Returns on capital have been remarkably steady for 5 years — durability is the real test of a moat
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
ROIC sits in the top quartile of Communication Services peers — the moat is wider than the neighbourhood

sect: Its 68% operating margin runs 59pp above the Communication Services median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 3.30x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 171 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 4% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 34% and a beta of 0.92, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.29 vs 5y 0.90), so read it loosely.
Trading is thin (about $68K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 49% in the 2020 crash and 54% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $13.52 (margin of safety -14%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 29%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $11.16 to $16.70 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Communication Services peers: P/E 20.0 vs 15.4, EV/EBITDA 19.0 vs 9.9 and P/FCF 18.5 vs 11.1 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.4% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 6.5% annual cash-flow growth, 2pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 508% clears the cost of capital of 9.2% by 499pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.07).
It converts 53% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.09x.
ROE of 264% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.6x equity multiplier).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $47.1M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 66.9, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 10.9% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 0% of profits supports about 1.9% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 3%.
It returns 5.2% a year to shareholders (3.3% in buybacks and 1.9% in dividends).
people: With about 935 employees, each generates about $601K of revenue, in line with the Communication Services median.
That works out to $319K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.1M (4x revenue per employee).
